To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the cardiac status of adolescents who have high blood pressure in childhood is normal in terms of ventricular size and wall thickness, but is abnormal in terms of cardiac performance.

the cardiac status of adolescents with high blood pressure since childhood is similar to that of adolescents with normal blood pressure, but that the cardiac status is consistent with previously reported observations of adults with essential hypertension, i.e. increased cardiac output and stroke volume with normal peripheral resistance.
children tracking with high blood pressures since early childhood have a greater cardiac performance at age 15 than children with low blood pressures over the same period.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long term effects of early childhood blood pressure on the heart in adolescence.

identifying the early changes that occur in the cardiovascular system of adolescents tracking in the upper percent of the blood pressure range for age, and with determining the factors that may be involved in the development of hypertension.
the relationship between blood pressure and cardiovascular structure and function in adolescents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children who have been in the upper 10% for blood pressure since early in childhood do not have a different echocardiographic profile than children who have been below the 10th percentile.
the cardiac status of the adolescents tracking with high or low blood pressure is normal.

the cardiac status of adolescents tracking in the upper percent of blood pressure since childhood is not different from those tracking in the lower percentiles of blood pressure, but that there are some changes in cardiac performance that may reflect the early changes of essential hypertension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cardiac changes in adolescents tracking with elevated blood pressure are not consistent with a hypertensive heart.

high blood pressure in childhood may be associated with a different pattern of cardiovascular risk factors than high blood pressure in adulthood, and that this pattern may be detectable in adolescence.
the cardiac status of adolescents tracking in the 80th percentile of blood pressure for age is not different than that of children in the lower 30th percentile for age.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no evidence of left ventricular hypertrophy in children tracking in the high blood-pressure range, but rather evidence of a normal increase in cardiac output.

the heart of adolescents with early onset of hypertension may be affected by the hypertension even at an early age, which is not necessarily the same for adults with hypertension, and this may be a reason for the different cardiovascular disease outcomes in children and adults with hypertension.
children in the upper blood pressure percentiles are more likely to have higher cardiac output and stroke volume than those in the lower percentiles.
